failure_summary.description: The answer carried a generic type word or descriptor already named by the clue's 'this X' phrase ('Sirius Satellite Radio', 'Roanoke Island'), or added middle initials to a person's name ('George H. W. Bush' vs 'George Bush').
The 'plural when the clue says these' rule produced 'tsunamis' where the key is the singular 'tsunami'.
The agent echoed a phrase from the clue instead of the referent: 'strange creatures' for an acronym expansion (Digital Monsters), and the tart's name for 'this season' (Fall).

No guidance for 'a part of this site' clues (answered the named building, not the containing site: Devereux Tower vs Tower of London), or for plain definition clues (answered 'quip' instead of the term whose definition matches both key descriptors: Epigram).

patch.reasoning: Two of the eight failures add extra words to the correct entity, and one pads a person's name. These are exact-match losses on answers that are otherwise right. The plural rule is also misleading for 'these' clues. The remaining misses repeat the clue's own words or an anchor (a building, an acronym's letters, a dish) instead of the referent, or pick a near-synonym for a definition clue. The edits strengthen the generic format rules, replace the wrong plural rule, and add a substitution test with container and definition handling. They do not add question-specific values.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Default to the singular, bare headword, even when the clue says 'these' or 'one of these' ('these destructive sea waves' -> 'Tsunami', not 'tsunamis'; 'Well', not 'wells'). Use the plural only for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas'), for things whose standard name is plural ('Giblets'), or when a verbatim archive/flashcard hit shows the plural.

edits.target: do not append that role word to the answer.
edits.content:
- Drop the generic type noun that the clue's 'this X' phrase already supplies, and drop corporate or descriptive suffixes. 'This island off North Carolina' -> 'Roanoke', not 'Roanoke Island'. 'This satellite radio company' -> 'Sirius', not 'Sirius Satellite Radio'. 'This river / lake / city / company / team' -> the bare name. Keep the type word only when it is inseparable from the standard name ('Hundred Years' War', 'World War II'). Test: put your answer in place of 'this X' in the clue. If a word is now repeated ('island ... Roanoke Island'), delete it.
- For people, use the plain 'First Last' form by which the person is commonly known, without middle names, initials or suffixes ('George Bush', not 'George H. W. Bush'). If the clue itself names the same person in some form, copy that form. A name form in a verbatim archive hit overrides this.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- SUBSTITUTION TEST: put your candidate in place of 'this X / these X / it' and reread the clue. The answer must be a member of the category X names (this season -> Fall/Winter/Spring/Summer; this island -> an island; these creatures -> a kind of creature). It must NOT be a phrase copied from the clue (a dish, a company, an event) or a word from the clue's own descriptors ('strange creatures'). Never answer with the clue's subject. The clue states a fact about the subject and asks for the thing the fact is tied to.
- '<Acronym or name> stands for ...' or 'short for ...' asks for the full expansion of the letters ('Digimon' -> 'Digital Monsters'). Give the expansion's words, not a descriptor from the clue. If a passage glosses the name ('Digimon: Digital Monsters'), copy that gloss.

edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content:
- Part vs whole: 'one of the buildings / rooms / towers at this site is named for X', 'a wing of this museum', or 'a gate of this city' asks for the WHOLE place that contains the named part ('Tower of London'), never the part itself ('Devereux Tower'). Passages that mention the part inside the larger place's page give the answer.
- Plain definition clues ('A short, witty saying', 'a crime for which ...', 'part of a racetrack ...') want the single dictionary term the definition fits best. Choose the headword whose definition matches ALL the clue's key words (short + witty + saying -> 'Epigram', whose entry reads 'a witty, ingenious, or pointed saying tersely expressed'), not a looser synonym ('quip'). Prefer the term whose dictionary/thesaurus/crossword snippet in the context nearly repeats the clue's wording.
